idiom_name: guard class with a private resource + policy check; java.lang.reflect.Proxy for transparent guards
implementation_notes: The JVM enforces field and method access at resolution ('access control ... to ensure that a reference to a class, interface, field, or method is permitted'), so a guard class with a private resource field and public methods that consult the policy before touching it is a real runtime boundary within the process - reflection being the documented exception, gated since Java 9 by the module system: setAccessible(true) 'cannot be used to enable access to private members ... when the declaring class is in a different module to the caller and the package containing the declaring class is not open to the caller's module'. The platform's own authorization layer is gone: SecurityManager was deprecated for removal in 17 (JEP 411) and JEP 486 permanently disabled it in JDK 24 - enabling it at startup is an error, AccessController.checkPermission always throws, and the JEP states it is 'not a goal to provide a replacement ... to sandbox Java code', directing sandboxing to containers and OS mechanisms. What remains for transparent protection proxies is java.lang.reflect.Proxy: 'static methods for creating objects that act like instances of interfaces but allow for customized method invocation', with every interface method dispatched to InvocationHandler.invoke where the policy is enforced before delegating.
pitfalls: The JVM's historical policy enforcement is unusable: SecurityManager is deprecated for removal and permanently disabled in JDK 24, so do not design new guards on AccessController/Policy - validate against the OS/container or a framework instead.

setAccessible(true) 'suppresses checks for Java language access control'; the surviving boundary is module encapsulation (exports vs opens), so the guard's package must be closed to reflection while its public API is exported.

A java.lang.reflect.Proxy class is defined by trusted system code and its ProtectionDomain is typically granted AllPermission - the proxy is a convenience, not a boundary; the guard's own check carries the claim.

Handler state is shared across calls: a singleton InvocationHandler holding one target leaks the last resource or crosses subjects between calls; create a handler per guarded resource and keep the target out of it.

variants.name: Dynamic protection proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy)
variants.implementation_notes: When callers already program against an interface, the JVM can generate the guard: Proxy.newProxyInstance creates an object that acts like an instance of that interface and dispatches every method call to InvocationHandler.invoke, where the policy is checked before method.invoke on the real object. The resource stays confined to the handler, the surface is exactly the interface the callers already use, and the same handler template serves several interfaces. The documented caveat is that the proxy class is defined by trusted system code (its protection domain is typically granted AllPermission) and its accessibility follows the least accessible proxy interface, so the guard's decision - not the proxy's provenance - is what enforces the policy.
pitfalls: The handler's method-name checks are coarse: overloads, default methods and Object methods (equals/hashCode/toString) arrive in the same invoke, so key the policy on the Method object and handle Object methods deliberately.
InvocationTargetException wraps whatever the target threw; unwrap it or the guard's error contract is not the resource's contract.

The generated proxy type follows the visibility of the least accessible interface: a package-private interface keeps the proxy unreachable outside the module, but a public one exposes the whole surface it proxies.

variants.name: JVM-mediated policy enforcement (legacy; deprecated and disabled)
variants.implementation_notes: The original Java realization put the owner outside the application: the JVM's SecurityManager pushed checkXxx calls into library code before sensitive operations, and the decision resolved through the caller's ProtectionDomain ('a set of classes whose instances are granted a set of permissions') and the installed Policy, evaluated by AccessController. Recorded here for legacy systems and for reading old policy files: it is deprecated for removal (JEP 411) and permanently disabled in JDK 24 (JEP 486) - enabling it at startup is an error, setSecurityManager throws UnsupportedOperationException, and AccessController.checkPermission always throws AccessControlException. New code must not build on it; the replacement direction is process/container/OS isolation.
pitfalls: Do not use this on modern JDKs: the API is non-functional (checkPermission always throws), the semantics cannot be relied on for tests, and Policy::setPolicy throws UnsupportedOperationException.

The old model walked the whole caller chain (stack walk), so its cost and failure modes differ completely from a guard-object check - retrofit notes that assume it 'answers per caller' are wrong once disabled.
Sandboxing Java code is now a container/OS concern; anything the application still needs must be re-expressed as an owning guard object or a framework authorization decision.
